A woman complained that unknown third parties had posted two ads on the Bakeca classifieds platform using her phone number, one in a massage category and one in an explicit 'love-meetings' category. The Garante found that Bakeca, as controller, had no technical or organisational measure to check that the user who entered a phone number actually owned it or was authorised by its holder. It also found the data was processed without a lawful basis, treating the number as special-category data given the sexual context. It ordered Bakeca to introduce verification measures for phone contacts in 'sensitive' ad categories and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000, plus publication of the decision.

The DPA held that a collection agency unlawfully disclosed the incorrect information about the existence of a debt to a data subject’s relatives, due to the possible foreclosure of an estate the data subject co-owned with their relatives.

The DPA reprimanded a credit information agency for improperly handling access requests. The controller referred data subjects to its data access portal without further action, and stated a fee would be charged for requests made more than once within 12 months.
The DPA fined a controller €60,000 for failing to comply with a corrective order requiring it to formalise and report its relationship with a processor.
The DPA warned two individuals to ensure their surveillance camera no longer films public roads after a neighbour complained about the camera capturing footage of them and the general public.

The Romanian DPA announced that it concluded an investigation at Altex România in January 2026. The investigation began after several data subjects complained about unanswered access and rectification requests, an account closure request and an erasure request. The authority found that the company did not respond to the authority's own investigative requests. It imposed four contravention fines totalling RON 40,768 (about EUR 8,000) for breaching Article 58(1) GDPR, in conjunction with Article 83(5)(e).
The DPA held that an employer sufficiently complied with an employee’s access request by providing personal data through reproduction rather than extraction of complete emails.

The DPA found that a lead generation company collecting professional contact data from LinkedIn complied with a prior decision ordering it to bring its data collection, data retention, transparency and access requests responses and activities into compliance. Therefore, the DPA did not enforce the penalty payment.
The DPA fined a transport services company €200,000 for obliging employees to use four tracking apps on their personal phones for work-related purposes.

The DPA fined two airline companies a total of €1,250,000 for unlawfully sharing employees' data between them after one airline purchased assets from the other. Further, the DPA found transparency violations connected to the shared data.

Two candidates who had passed a public recruitment competition run by the Ministry complained that the final ranking list, published online by the Ministry's processor Formez PA, contained excessive personal data, including tax codes, intermediate scores and an indication of preference/precedence grounds. One complainant also got a late reply to an erasure request. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 6, 9 and 12 GDPR and the Italian Code. It fined the Ministry EUR 15,000, rating gravity as medium, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed as the unlawful publication had ended.

A municipal police force reported that a cooperative providing cleaning and maintenance services had installed fingerprint readers to record the working hours of six employees. The company ignored the Garante's request for information, and an inspection confirmed the biometric system had run since 1 September 2024. No information notice was given, and no impact assessment or record of processing existed. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a),(c), 9, 13, 30 and 35 GDPR and of Article 157 of the Code. It banned further processing, ordered deletion of the biometric data within 60 days and fined the company EUR 15,000.

A complainant whose mobile number was on the Public Opposition Register received unwanted pre-recorded and follow-up promotional calls for a water-treatment business. The business had bought leads from Flamel S.r.l., which said it acted as processor. The Garante found that Flamel processed personal data without a proper formal appointment as processor and breached the processor obligations of Article 28, including engaging a sub-processor without the controller's authorisation. It fined Flamel EUR 15,000, ordered publication of the decision on its website and noted it in its internal register.

A candidate in a public competition for 38 senior civil-service posts complained about the handling of her data on the recruitment platform run by Formez PA, the Ministry's processor. Formez PA published online the names of over 300 candidates admitted to the written tests, and the Ministry posted a link to that list on its own website. The Garante found the publication unlawful (no legal basis, breach of lawfulness and processor oversight) but found no proof that the complainant's health data had been published. It fined the Ministry EUR 12,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed because the Ministry removed the link and had Formez PA remove the lists once the investigation began.

A man complained that an online news article from 2016 about his arrest for car theft remained online and that his erasure request of December 2023 went unanswered. The publisher's contact email for such requests had been inactive for years, and the company also ignored the Garante's request for information. The Garante found breaches of Article 12(2) and (3) GDPR and of Article 157 of the Italian Code. It noted that the data had been removed from the article and the article de-indexed. It ordered the company to put in place measures to handle data subject requests and fined it EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

Eleven health authorities in Emilia Romagna notified a personal data breach. A maintenance update by their software supplier, Dedalus Italia, to the staff portal application WHR-Time removed a search filter. For a few hours, employees could see their colleagues' active absence and attendance requests, including requests under Law 104/1992 that concern relatives and minors. The Garante found that Dedalus, as processor, had not put in place technical and organisational measures adequate to the risks, in breach of Article 32 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 32,000 and ordered publication of the order. It imposed no further corrective measures because the conduct had ended and the company had adopted measures.

The DPA warned a company for failing to provide a job applicant with the recording of their job interview. Instead of complying with the respective access request, the controller deleted the file after receiving the applicant’s request.

The DPA ordered Amazon to limit the processing of its employees’ personal data on a platform that allowed managers to add comments on employees’ individual files, as well as the processing of personal data by cameras placed in areas reserved for employees.

The UK Information Commissioner investigated Reddit as part of its work on conformance with the Children's Code. It found that Reddit processed children's personal data, including that of children under 13, without a lawful basis and without fairness or transparency, and without valid parental consent. It also found that Reddit failed to carry out a data protection impact assessment for the high-risk processing of children's data from 25 May 2018 to 31 December 2024. The Commissioner imposed a penalty of £14,472,500, set as separate fines for the processing infringements and the DPIA infringement.

An employee of KEAT asked twice in June and July 2023 for the CCTV footage of an incident in the centre's courtyard and received no answer. Footage from only one of two cameras was supplied late, after the HDPA intervened, and it had been processed (zoomed). The HDPA found breaches of the access right (Art. 15 with Art. 12(3)) and of Art. 24, since staff were not trained to handle such requests. It fined the controller EUR 5,000 for the access breach, reprimanded it for Art. 24, and ordered it to supply the requested footage within 15 days.

The Hungarian authority investigated the University of Szeged's dormitory admission process for the 2022-2024 academic years, including the social-situation assessment of applicants. It found that the university negligently breached the data protection principles (fairness/transparency and data minimisation), lacked a proper legal basis, mishandled special-category data and gave inadequate information to applicants. It ordered the university to stop the unlawful processing, delete the unlawfully held data and provide proper information, and imposed a fine of HUF 2,000,000. The decision is to be published on the authority's website.

The DPA reprimanded the City of London Police for its failure to respond to data subjects’ access requests in time. The DPA’s investigation covered requests related to law enforcement matters as well as non-law enforcement related matters.

The DPA fined a private university HUF 2,000,000 (approximately €5,286) for processing excessive data of students applying for accommodation scholarships. The DPA considered that the university had processed data beyond what was necessary under national law.
The DPA fined a company PLN 5,898,064 (approximately €1,392,768) for unlawfully collecting images and scans of ID cards and passports from the users of its application for fraud prevention purposes.
The DPA fined a police officer €200 for unlawfully accessing the data of a data subject for purposes unrelated to their work duties.

At a press conference on 6 May 2025 a member of parliament presented to journalists a pre-sale property contract and a handwritten will, which contained personal data of two private individuals, including PESEL numbers, ID numbers and addresses. The election committee of a presidential candidate was held responsible for this unlawful disclosure. The UODO President found breaches of Article 6(1) and Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. He imposed an administrative fine of PLN 35,582 (about EUR 8,470), calculated using EDPB Guidelines 04/2022 and reduced heavily for proportionality. The decision is not yet final.

The DPA fined a hospital €6,000 for unlawfully installing video surveillance cameras in operating rooms and staff workplaces without a valid legal basis, and for storing the data for excessively long periods.

A municipal employee complained that the Municipality of Coccaglio used video surveillance footage from its municipal warehouse for disciplinary charges, without proper information, retention periods or the labour-law safeguards. The Garante found that four cameras were installed and operated without a trade union agreement or labour inspectorate authorisation, that the footage was used for disciplinary purposes, and that information and a DPIA were lacking. Because the municipality had switched off the system, cooperated and signed a union agreement, no further corrective measures were ordered. A fine of EUR 6,000 was imposed and the decision is to be published.

A former freelance IT consultant complained that Based s.r.l. gave an inadequate reply to his request for access to, and erasure of, the company email account assigned to him during his engagement. The company had disabled the account after the contract ended, kept it until January 2025 and deleted it, so access could no longer be given. It also never gave him a privacy notice. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 12, 13, 15 and 17 GDPR and ordered the company to pay a fine of EUR 12,000, with publication of the order.

A complainant whose number was on the Public Opposition Register received an unwanted promotional call made for a water purification company. The data had been collected via a sign-up form on a website run by the list provider Unleadmited, which sold the leads on. The Garante found the consent and legal basis inadequate, the accountability measures insufficient, the information notice and forms deficient on transparency, and that Unleadmited had failed to answer the Authority's request for information on time. It declared the processing unlawful, banned further use of the data collected through the website, ordered compliance, and fined the company EUR 5,000 with publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA investigated a water-purification company after a complaint from a person whose number was on the Public Opposition Register and who received an unwanted promotional call. The company had bought a contact list from a lead-generation group and could not show valid consent or that it had clearly identified the roles of the companies involved. The Garante found breaches of lawfulness, accountability, consent and controller/processor role rules, and fined the company EUR 15,000. It also banned further use of data held without a valid legal basis and ordered corrective measures, plus publication of the decision.

An insurance intermediary, acting as agent of an insurance company, sent promotional emails to customers without consent, using data it held as processor. A complainant also got no reply to an access request. The Garante found the company had acted as an autonomous controller and had breached the principles of lawfulness and transparency, the consent rules, information duties and access rights. It fined the company EUR 15,000 (0.33% of turnover), banned secondary and marketing use of the data without valid consent, ordered a reply to the second complainant, and ordered publication of the decision.

A former member of the GetFIT gyms complained that he kept receiving marketing emails, an SMS and a paper letter after objecting and asking for erasure. The company admitted that manual alignment between its CRM and its email-marketing providers failed, and that it had not answered the Garante's request for information. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 17 GDPR and of Articles 130 and 157 of the Italian Code, but no breach of Article 31 GDPR because the company cooperated. It imposed a fine of EUR 30,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the company had automated its database alignment.

Two lawyers complained to the Garante that Lex Iuris, a legal training company, sent them an unsolicited promotional email on 25 November 2024 and did not answer their access requests. The company said it had used email addresses collected to propose teaching collaborations by human error, and that it lacked a system to track data subject requests. The Garante found a breach of Article 6(1)(a) GDPR and Article 130(2) of the Code for the marketing emails, but treated it as a minor violation and only issued a reprimand. For failing to answer the access requests (Articles 12 and 15) it imposed a fine of EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A customer complained that Vodafone Panafon did not properly answer her repeated requests for access to recordings of her calls about a technical fault. The company rejected the first two requests as incomplete, asked her to specify dates, and finally supplied 18 recordings from 25-11-2021 onward, while earlier calls were lost under its 12-month retention. The Authority found infringements of Articles 12(1)-(4), 15 and 18 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 30,000 and ordered the company to take technical and organisational measures, including better staff training, to handle data subject requests properly and on time.
The DPA warned a laundry company after it failed to comply with an access request from an alleged customer who received several inexplicable invoices.

The DPA partially upheld a complaint and issued a reprimand against a travel company for unlawful direct marketing, excessive passport copy collection, inaccuracies in travel documents, lack of transparency, and an incomplete response to an access request.
The DPA issued a warning to the Federal Public Service for Finances after an employee unlawfully accessed the address of an individual in the controller’s database and visited her at her home.

ANSPDCP investigated Tensa Art Design S.A after a user complained that its website lensa.ro placed tracking and behavioural advertising cookies. The investigation found that the company did not reply to the authority's request made in the exercise of its investigative powers. It was fined 101,794 lei (about EUR 20,000) for breaching Article 83(5)(e) read with Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR. A corrective measure ordered it to send the requested response to the authority.

The Hungarian authority examined Óbuda University's dormitory admission and social-situation assessment process for the 2022-2024 academic years. It found that the university negligently breached the transparency and data minimisation principles, processed data without a legal basis and lacked a condition for processing special-category (health) data, because it requested certificates and documents it was not entitled to. The authority issued a finding against the university, banned this collection going forward, ordered deletion of unlawfully processed data, and imposed a fine of HUF 1,500,000. The decision is to be published on the authority's website.

The DPA reprimanded a trade union for processing information about an employee’s salary in order to analyse the workplace’s compliance with legal equal treatment provisions during the course of collective bargaining procedures.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation in December 2025 into Genpact Romania SRL, which had notified a personal data breach caused by a cyber attack. Attackers exploited weak passwords and the account authentication reset process of a compromised user account, exposing employee data of a significant number of people across the EU. The authority found the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures under Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of RON 50,899 (about EUR 10,000), which the company has already paid.

The DPA fined a platform operator GBP 247,590 (approximately €282,917) for the unlawful processing of children’s personal data, the lack of age verification and measures to obtain parental consent, and a failure to carry out an impact assessment.

The DPA held that a guardianship authority had violated the GDPR by unlawfully disclosing the residential address of a parent and his two minor children to their estranged grandparent. The address information was not necessary for client identification, and the authority lacked legal basis for the disclosure.

The Dutch DPA investigated how the Delft municipal executive processed personal data in a 'power-field analysis' (krachtenveldanalyse) of the Islamic community. It found the executive processed personal data without an adequate legal basis, and also processed special-category data without an exception to the prohibition. This breached the lawfulness principle read with Articles 6(1) and 9(1) GDPR. The AP imposed an administrative fine of EUR 25,000, deviating from the amounts in its fining policy rules for public bodies. It also imposed a processing restriction: the analysis may be kept only to facilitate data subject rights and for legal proceedings.

The Dutch DPA fined the executive board of the municipality of Zoetermeer EUR 25,000. The municipality held a 'krachtenveldanalyse' (power-structure analysis of the local Muslim community) containing personal data, including special-category data, without a valid legal basis or an exception to the ban on special-category data. The AP departed from its standard fine amounts for public bodies. It took into account that the situation was one-off, short-lived, involved a relatively limited number of data subjects, and arose in a complex political climate. The municipality had destroyed all copies, apologised, and admitted the violations.
The DPA found that the food delivery company Wolt failed to respond properly and in time to a customer’s access request after their account was blocked.
The DPA ordered a landlord to erase the data provided by potential tenants after not entering into a lease agreement with them.

The Hungarian authority examined how the university MATE handled data in its dormitory admission and related social-situation assessment procedures for the 2022-2024 academic years. It found that the university negligently breached the principles of fairness/transparency and data minimisation, lacked a proper legal basis for some data it collected, and gave inadequate information to applicants. It issued a reprimand, banned the unlawful processing and ordered deletion of the unlawfully held data, ordered the privacy notice to be corrected, and imposed a fine of HUF 1,500,000.

The DPA fined the Hungarian University HUF 1,500,000 (€3,933.80) for the unlawful, excessive and insufficiently transparent data processing in course of dormitory admissions. According to the DPA, the university incorrectly referred to consent in its admission forms.

The DPA issued a reprimand to 51 municipalities and simultaneously warned them regarding their use of Google’s products in primary and lower secondary schools. In particular, the DPA found that the municipalities had not adequately demonstrated an adequate level of protection for personal data processed outside the EU.

A patient complained that her photographs from a rhinoseptoplasty were posted on a surgeon's public Instagram profile, captioned as published with her consent. The surgeon relied on a consent form supplied by the professional association AICPE and argued the images were anonymous. The Garante found the patient identifiable, the anonymisation ineffective and the consent invalid because it was given on the premise of anonymous publication. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the surgeon EUR 5,000, ordered him to rewrite his information and consent forms within 90 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A parent complained that a school published on its website a circular listing 51 pupils with disabilities, with their classes, the times of their inclusion working group (GLO) meetings and their support teachers. The school said it was a material error: the circular was meant only for teachers, and the PDF stayed on the server after the page was removed. The Garante found that the information reveals health data, was disclosed without a legal basis and that this breached Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 9 GDPR and the related Code provisions. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000, taking into account the school's small size, quick removal, cooperation and corrective measures, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended.

Parents of a pupil injured at school complained that the school held a video of the incident, filmed with a phone from a screen showing CCTV footage and handed to a private investigator hired by the insurer. The Garante found that the school's CCTV system, running since 2019 including in daytime with minors and staff present, had no valid legal basis (legitimate interest not available), breached the labour-law safeguards of Art. 4 of Law 300/1970, lacked adequate transparency and had no DPIA. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the congregation's province EUR 12,000. No further corrective measures were ordered because the cameras had been switched off and litigation was pending.

The Garante was alerted that e-Campus, an online university, used facial recognition to identify and check attendance of participants in a teacher-qualification course, relying on student consent presented as mandatory. The investigation showed biometric processing from March to November 2024. The Garante held that consent cannot be the legal basis for a university's public-interest processing, that the processing of biometric data lacked a valid legal basis and breached minimisation, storage limitation, data protection by design and DPIA obligations. It declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 50,000 with publication, and no further corrective measures since the conduct had ended.

An employee of a national archaeological museum complained that he received a disciplinary measure based on video surveillance footage from cameras installed without respecting labour-law safeguards and without adequate transparency. The Garante found that the Ministry of Culture ran the system without a union agreement or authorisation until 25 June 2025, without a legal basis, with inadequate information to data subjects and workers, and without a prior DPIA. One camera also filmed a public street and a private building. Treating it as a single conduct, it imposed a single fine of EUR 12,000 and ordered publication, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ceased.

The DPA held that health data that is required for an expert opinion in a court proceeding can be processed under Article 9(2)(f) GDPR and Article 9(2)(g) GDPR in conjunction with Austrian national law and, the selection of relevant data is at the discretion of the expert.
The DPA issued a warning to an employer to ensure compliance of its processing activities after one of its managers shared an employee’s resignation in a work-related group chat.

The DPA warned a football club to ensure that it only processed relevant and necessary personal data for tickets cancellation. Furthermore, in relation to security measures for matches, the DPA warned the club to ensure it only processed personal data when it has a valid legal basis.

Sportadmin provides web-based administration and a mobile app for sports clubs. An attacker used an SQL injection through an unprotected variable introduced in code in June 2022 and gained access to its servers, with the data later published on the Darknet. IMY found that Sportadmin had not taken appropriate technical and organisational security measures, in breach of Article 32(1) GDPR. It treated the company and its parent group as one undertaking, set the fine on the group's turnover, and found the infringement of high gravity because over two million people, mostly children, were exposed. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 6,000,000, with the company's active role towards the clubs after the incident counted in its favour.
The DPA held that the usage of a bodycam on private property in a purely private setting falls under the household exemption in Article 2(2)(c) GDPR.

France Travail, the French public employment operator, suffered an intrusion between 6 February and 5 March 2024. Attackers used social engineering to take over accounts of CAP EMPLOI advisers and reach job-seekers' data, including identification data and the social security number (NIR). After an inspection, the CNIL restricted committee found a breach of Article 32 GDPR (security of processing) and called it serious negligence. It rejected the argument that a public body cannot be fined, because the processing was carried out on behalf of the State rather than by the State. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000,000, an injunction with a EUR 5,000 daily penalty on password policy, multifactor authentication, activity-log monitoring and access rights, and publication of the decision. France Travail will cease to be named two years after publication.

The DPA ruled that Microsoft Corporation unlawfully installed tracking cookies on a pupil’s device when using Microsoft 365 Education without valid consent and ordered the company to cease such processing.

The DPA fined a digital marketing agency €25,500 for recording and indefinitely storing applicants’ phone interviews without a valid legal basis or telling them about the recording and the identity of the actual controller.

After the controller notified a personal data breach, ANSPDCP investigated and finished in December 2025. An Excel file listing employees, including medical data from medical certificates of current and former staff, was repeatedly circulated internally. The authority found breaches of the data minimisation and accountability principles and of the security obligations. It imposed two fines of the equivalent of EUR 5,000 and EUR 10,000 (EUR 15,000 total) and a corrective measure to put in place technical and organisational procedures, with monitoring, to detect breaches immediately.

In addition, the DPA fined a bank €400.000 for allowing numerous of its controller’s staff members to access its CCTV system using a single shared username and password in violation of Article 32 GDPR.

The DPA found that the provider of an online shop for protective masks violated its information obligations by placing cookies on a data subject’s device without displaying a cookie banner or providing a publicly accessible privacy policy.

The DPA imposed a fine of NOK 250,000 (€25,000) on a provider of a time-recording systems which claimed to be just a processor when in fact it was determining the purposes and means of the processing. Further, the provider failed to provide 80 data subjects with access to their time records after their employer went bankrupt.

The DPA fined a company GBP 120,000 (approximately €138,000) for unlawfully sending over 4 million unsolicited marketing text messages to individuals with the aim of promoting the services of a different company.

After the controller notified a personal data breach, the Romanian authority investigated and found that a cyber attack on the controller's application led to unauthorised access to employees' personal data. The controller had not implemented adequate technical and organisational security measures and had not ensured that it used only processors giving sufficient guarantees. It was fined RON 40,736 (about EUR 8,000) as a contravention sanction, which it has paid.

The DPA fined a medical student €200 for filming a hospital patient with dementia and sharing the video with a fellow student. It found that the recording and disclosure constituted unlawful processing of health data.

The DPA fined a financial institution €8,000 for requesting unnecessary photographs of data subjects holding their ID when they wanted to cancel a loan. The DPA ordered the use of less intrusive verification methods.
The AEPD fined a political party €500 for publishing a document on Facebook that showed a person’s name, ID number and signature without a legal basis under Article 6 GDPR.

The DSB held that a therapy association violated a patient's right of access by failing to disclose personal data in a therapist's handwritten notes and by omitting required information on purposes, categories, recipients and retention.

The President of UODO fined the Kraków City Police Commander a total of PLN 78,000 for publishing in a press release the personal data of a woman, including health data, whom police had questioned in 2023 about who helped her have an abortion, and for lacking proper oversight of data processing. The press release contained special-category data on her mental and physical state, treatment, reproductive health and suspected offences, and was only partly trimmed an hour later. The press team processed data without considering risks to individuals, and the technical and organisational measures were not regularly tested or evaluated. The controller itself notified the breach, but the data was used for a purpose other than the one it was collected for and its disclosure was not necessary.

In October 2024 an attacker broke into Free Mobile's information system and obtained subscriber data, in a breach that ran from 28 September to 22 October 2024. The company notified the CNIL, which received over 2,600 complaints and carried out an inspection. The restricted committee found breaches of Articles 5(1)(e), 32 and 34 GDPR (retention, security and information of data subjects). It fined Free Mobile EUR 27 million, calculated on the turnover of the parent group Iliad as a single economic unit, because the data of over 24 million contracts were affected. It also ordered compliance with a daily penalty of EUR 50,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA issued a €15,000,000 fine to a landline telephone provider for insufficient security measures and for failing to provide all necessary information to data subjects following a data breach affecting 7 million data subjects.

A fire service officer complained that her illness, treatment and medication were written in detail in the Daily Order book of her local fire station and in documents posted on the Fire Service's electronic document system, accessible to many staff. The Authority found that this health data was processed unlawfully and beyond what was necessary. It held the Fire Service Headquarters to be the controller and found breaches of the lawfulness and data minimisation principles. It also noted that the rule keeping Daily Order books forever breaches the storage limitation principle and should be amended. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000.
The DPA reprimanded an employer for unlawfully maintaining the email accounts of a former employee and for a failure to comply with the employee’s access and deletion requests.

The Croatian DPA carried out an unannounced inspection of a shop in a shopping centre and found seven CCTV cameras with no notice anywhere saying the premises were under video surveillance. The controller had already been fined in December 2022 for the same failure at another location. The Agency found a violation of Article 27(1) of the Croatian GDPR Implementation Act and imposed the maximum fine of EUR 6,636.14, treating the repeat offence as intentional and as a significant aggravating factor.

The DPA fined the national postal operator €232,000 for appointing a DPO with a conflict of interest. The DPO concurrently served as a Security Director and representative of the controller, effectively monitoring their own decisions regarding the means of data processing.
The DPA fined a company €1,282 for a failure to conclude a data processing agreement required under Article 28(3) GDPR with its processor.

The DPA fined a gambling operator €2.59 m for processing biometric data without valid consent and beyond the necessary scope, bundling multiple purposes into single consent, and providing incomplete and inconsistent processing information.

The Greek DPA examined numerous complaints about unsolicited marketing calls made for the gas supplier ZENITH by external call centres, including calls to numbers in the Article 11 opt-out register. It found that ZENITH failed to take adequate measures to monitor its processors (Article 32) and fined it EUR 10,000, ordered it to set up call-centre audit procedures within six months, and reprimanded it for a call to a former customer without a legal basis (Articles 5 and 6). The three call-centre processors were also fined (One Way Private Company EUR 40,000 as processor plus EUR 40,000 as controller, Sigma & Kappa EUR 10,000, Revma Plus EUR 5,000), and One Way was ordered to destroy data lacking valid consent.

The Greek DPA examined numerous complaints about marketing calls made for the gas supplier ZENITH, including calls to numbers listed in the Article 11 opt-out register. The calls were made by ZENITH's call-centre processors (One Way, Sigma & Kappa Eisagogiki, Revma Plus), often through manual dialling errors or technical failures. The Authority found security failures (Art. 32) by ZENITH and the three call centres. It also found that One Way, as controller, breached Articles 29, 5, 6 and 7 on the validity of consent. ZENITH received a EUR 10,000 fine, a reprimand and orders to put in place checks on its call centres. One Way received two fines of EUR 40,000 each (EUR 80,000 in total) and an order to destroy data collected without valid consent. Sigma & Kappa received EUR 10,000 and Revma Plus EUR 5,000.

The Authority examined many complaints about unsolicited marketing calls made for the gas supplier ZENITH by external call centres. A joint decision covers ZENITH and three call-centre processors: One Way, Sigma & Kappa and Revma Plus. For Sigma & Kappa, numbers on the Article 11 opt-out register were called manually by mistake. The Authority found a breach of Article 32 GDPR, fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered it to put in place the control procedures described in Thought 20 within six months. The other companies received their own separate fines and corrective measures.

The Authority examined many complaints about marketing calls made for the gas supplier ZENITH by its call-centre processors, including calls to numbers listed in the Article 11 opt-out register. It found security failings (Article 32) on the part of ZENITH and three call centres, among them Revma Plus. For Revma Plus, the calls came from human error in manual dialling and from a technical fault that failed to exclude registered numbers. The Authority fined Revma Plus EUR 5,000 under Article 32 and ordered it to implement the procedures described in its reasoning within six months. ZENITH, One Way and S&K were sanctioned in the same decision; only the Revma Plus part is summarised here.

The DPA fined a gas supplier €10,000 for failing to supervise its processors and for calling formers customers after contract termination without a legal basis. The DPA also fined the supplier’s processors €40,000, €10,000, and €5,000 for ineffective safeguards that allowed systematic calls to numbers registered in the opt-out registry.
The DPA fined a company RON 50,920 (€10,000) for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in light of repeated data breaches affecting its customers.

After repeated cyber attacks on its IT platform, the retailer Roumasport S.R.L notified personal data breaches to the Romanian authority. The investigation found that customer accounts were accessed without authorisation because the company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures. Customer data such as names, contact details, passwords and purchase history were exposed. The authority fined the company 50,920 lei, equivalent to EUR 10,000.

Following an online and on-site CNIL inspection in January 2023 of a retailer with a loyalty programme of about 10.5 million members, the restricted committee found breaches of GDPR Articles 6, 13, 32 and 35 and of Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act. The company had passed loyalty members' contact data to a social network group for targeted advertising from late 2018 until February 2024 without informed consent, clear information or a prior impact assessment, and had security and cookie shortcomings. The committee fined it EUR 3.5 million in total (EUR 2.5 million for the GDPR breaches, EUR 1 million for the cookie rule). No injunction was issued because the company had come into compliance, and the decision is published without naming the company.

The DPA found that a hospital unlawfully carried out video surveillance and audio recording in several areas, including operating rooms. While video surveillance in general hospital areas could be justified by legitimate interests, monitoring in operating rooms and certain patient examination areas was deemed unlawful processing of health data.

NEXPUBLICA FRANCE publishes and hosts the PCRM software used by the Nord departmental disability office (MDPH). Two incidents in October-November 2022, caused by configuration errors, let portal users see data of third parties, in one case the data of 14,170 people. After an inspection, the CNIL restricted committee found that the company failed to ensure adequate security under Article 32 GDPR. It rejected the company's fair-trial and proportionality arguments. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 1,700,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with the company no longer named after two years.

The DPA issued a reprimand to a hospital for failing to implement sufficient measures for managing access to electronic health records after a physiotherapist accessed information on the sex of an unborn child and revealed it to the mother.

A complainant received a traffic-code notice after a licence-plate reading camera operated by the municipality of Nave flagged her vehicle, and her erasure request went unanswered. The Garante found that the municipality ran three plate-reading gates continuously, storing all passing vehicle data for seven days, without a valid legal basis. It also found a lack of transparency, no data protection impact assessment, and no reply to the data subject's request. It fined the municipality EUR 6,000 and ordered it to survey its cameras, define purposes and legal bases, carry out or update the DPIA and revise its privacy notices. The decision is to be published.

An employee complaint led the Garante to inspect Pioneer Hi-Bred Italia Sementi, which had installed satellite telematics devices on company cars to score employees' driving behaviour, including on private trips. The Authority found the privacy notice inadequate, no proper legitimate-interest balancing, processors not properly appointed under Article 28, and breaches of the employment-law rules (Articles 113 and 114 of the Code, Article 88 GDPR). It ordered deletion of the data on private trips and imposed a fine of EUR 120,000. The decision is also to be published on the Garante's website.

A former employee complained that his employer, Anticimex, did not answer his access request under Article 15 within the deadline. The investigation also showed that the company kept his work mailbox active after he left and had a superior read it to gather evidence for a court case against him, with inadequate information notices. The Garante found breaches of the GDPR principles, transparency, access and employment-data provisions and of Article 114 of the Italian Code. It banned access to employees' email (except for the complainant's account for defending rights in court), ordered the company to bring its information notices into line within 60 days, and fined it EUR 40,000.

A former managing director of LTL S.p.A. complained that, after his dismissal, his individualised company email account stayed active and kept receiving messages, and that the company ignored his request of 22 September 2023 to access the correspondence and deactivate the account. The Garante found that the company never answered the access request within the one-month deadline and kept and accessed the mailbox for about two months after employment ended, breaching the processing principles. It ordered the company to give the complainant the information requested and to delete the mailbox content, apart from what is needed for legal defence, and imposed a fine of EUR 40,000. The complaint about Instagram access linked to the work SIM was not found to show a violation.

Two joint controllers received a reprimand after their shared website deployed a cookie banner that blocked users from reading the cookie policy and provided contradictory information about the identity of the data controller.
The DPA fined an energy supplier €30,000 for not verifying data concerning a customer energy connection, resulting in a change of the energy supplier for the wrong person.

The DPA fined a private tutoring centre €4,000 for non-compliance with a parent’s request to access personal data concerning his two minor children and for the lack of cooperation with the DPA during the investigation.

The DPA reprimanded a clinic for sharing 23 years' worth of medical records based on a patient’s request to transmit the records of the last 5 years to their insurer. Furthermore, the DPA found that the clinic failed to ensure security of processing and to report a data breach in time.

The DPA held that under Article 15 GDPR, a data subject cannot request that the bar association provides them with a copy of entire documents containing information about a third party, i.e. the lawyer reported to the bar by the data subject. Therefore, the DPA also considered the confidentiality of the disciplinary proceedings against the lawyer.

In 2021 a hacker used SQL injection through a web form to reach a database server of the HAN university and demanded a ransom. The Dutch DPA investigated not the breach itself but whether the security measures before it were adequate. It found they were not appropriate to the risk, so Article 32 GDPR was infringed. It set a base fine of EUR 310,000 under its 2019 fining guidelines and reduced it to EUR 175,000 because of the HAN's mitigation efforts, an information security project already under way, and its outreach to other organisations. The HAN admitted the infringement and, according to the press release, will not object.

The ICO found that Police Scotland, when preparing misconduct packs, breached the Data Protection Act 2018 (sections 35 and 37) in its mobile phone data extraction. It also breached the UK GDPR on security, data minimisation, data protection by design and breach notification. In one incident, a complainant's mobile phone extraction data was wrongly disclosed to a third party, and the breach was not reported within 72 hours. The ICO issued a reprimand for the DPA infringements and a single penalty of £66,000 for the UK GDPR infringements. The public sector approach meant no fine for the DPA infringements, although the ICO had initially considered one of £78,750.

Deezer notified the CNIL of a data breach in November 2022 that pointed to its former processor, Mobius Solutions (Optimove), an Israeli marketing-tool company with no EU establishment. After an inspection, the CNIL's restricted committee held that the GDPR applies under Article 3(2)(b) because the company's segmentation of Deezer users amounts to behavioural profiling. It found breaches of Articles 28, 29 and 30 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 1,000,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with the company no longer named after two years.
The DPA fined a company GBP 105,000 (approximately €120,000) for sending over 67 million unsolicited direct marketing emails to data subjects without consent or a valid exception.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation in November 2025 into Crowd Entertainment Limited after a data subject complained about how their access request was handled. The operator could not show it had given a complete and proper written reply within the legal time limit, covering the complainant's player accounts on its platforms and information on self-exclusion requests. It was fined 76,333 lei (about EUR 15,000) and ordered to give a full reply to the request and to put in place technical and organisational measures, including staff training and involvement of the DPO, so that data subject requests are handled correctly and on time.

The DPA reprimanded and fined a university €98,000 following six data breaches after it failed to take appropriate measures to ensure security of processing, to keep a record of processing activities, and to comply with its notification obligations.

The DPA issued a warning to Medex to ensure appropriate technical and organisational measures for the transmission of medical records after the loss and misplacement of several medical records, as well as for the failure to notify the loss of one of the records to the DPA.

A complainant said the municipality of Tuscania ran about 50 street cameras, with licence-plate reading, plus cameras at waste collection points, with no signage or full privacy notice. The municipality had also refused an access request and had not signed processor agreements. The Garante found that the urban-security pact with the Prefecture did not identify the cameras or areas covered, so there was no valid legal basis. It also found transparency failures, no DPIA, no Article 28 arrangements, an unlawful refusal of access, and incomplete compliance with an earlier Garante order. It fined the municipality EUR 12,000 in total for two separate conducts and ordered it to stop processing and delete the plate data and to review all its cameras.

The DPA fined a school €1,000 for unlawfully disclosing students’ personal data by sending an email about vaccination obligations in which all recipients’ email addresses were visible. The DPA held that the indication that students had not received specific vaccinations constituted unlawful processing of sensitive data.
The DPA fined a customer support provider €80,000 for unlawfully transferring its employees’ private phone numbers to its business customer without a valid legal basis.
The DPA held that a data subject had manifestly made their health data public by disclosing an ADHD diagnosis on a publicly accessible forum, even though the post was published under a pseudonym.

The DPA held that the Ministry of Education and Sports of Andalusia’s provision of cloud-based educational services to public schools violated GDPR provisions relating to transparency, privacy by design, international data transfers and DPIA duties. The Ministry used Microsoft as a processor for this activity.

The DPA fined two so-called 'sovereign citizens' and founding members of an organisation providing identity documents for a non-existing state €1,300 each. The organisation processed personal data without a valid legal basis and did not provide data subjects with adequate information.

The DPA issued a reprimand to a company for unlawfully transmitting information on a former employee in a phone conversation with another company during a recruitment process. The DPA also reprimanded both companies for failing to respond to access requests.

The DPA fined a sports retail company €2,600,000 after personal data of more than 6 million people was published in the dark web in course of a ransomware attack. The DPA found that the company lacked adequate security measures under Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.
The DPA fined a credit card company €1.5 million for placing optional cookies without consent on users’ devices and for not deleting them when users withdrew their consent.
The DPA fined a data broker €40,000 for unlawfully reselling personal data it purchased from a phone company to another company carrying out direct marketing activities.

The Italian DPA examined a complaint and a later report from a former and a prospective customer of a home security company who kept receiving promotional SMS and calls after asking for erasure and objecting to marketing. It found that the company answered the rights requests late, collected invalid consent for marketing through its website quote box, and breached storage limitation and information duties on retention periods. It fined the company EUR 400,000 (0.18% of turnover), ordered a ban on marketing use of the data obtained without valid consent, deletion of that data, and corrected privacy notices. Publication of the decision was ordered as an ancillary sanction. Some complaints, on telebooking and former-customer legal bases, were closed.

The Italian DPA investigated Aimag S.p.A., a water and waste utility, after a report that anyone could register on its website's customer area using only a tax code and any email address, with no identity check. The inspection also found pre-ticked consent boxes for marketing, unclear privacy notices and a five-year retention period for marketing data. The Garante found violations of security, lawful basis, transparency and storage-limitation rules. It ordered Aimag to adopt adequate security measures and to update its consent wording and privacy notice, and imposed a fine of EUR 300,000 plus publication of the decision.
The DPA issued a warning against the University of Turin for failing to instruct a researcher on how to administer a survey collecting sensitive data.

The DPA held that an organisation could retain a job applicant’s personal data after their rejection, as doing so served its legitimate interest in defending itself against possible legal claims raised by the applicant. In particular, the DPA considered that the applicant already announced legal action against the controller.

The DPA held that an online store unlawfully required customers to select their gender identity. According to the DPA, this was not necessary for the proper performance of a contract with its customers or for its legitimate interest to personally address them.

The DPA fined a communication network provider €4,500,000 for several GDPR breaches including unlawful data transfers to Serbia and for misleading users with vague information that hid regular third-country processing.

The DPA held that the deletion of personal data by the controller during the proceedings constituted a violation of the data subject's right of access under Article 15 in conjunction with Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.

The DPA refused to handle a complaint filed by a data subject against the court-appointed expert who prepared an opinion on contract arrangement in a joint custody case. According to the DPA, the complaint was abusive since it was aimed to delegitimize the expert’s work rather than data protection reasons.

Following a second complaint from the NOYB association, the CNIL carried out online inspections of the Vanity Fair website run by Les Publications Condé Nast. It found that the company placed an advertising cookie (NID) before any consent, and that the cookie banner gave wrong information about cookies presented as strictly necessary. Other shortcomings concerned the collection of consent and the handling of refusal and withdrawal (the excerpt does not cover these in full). The restricted committee fined the company EUR 750,000 for breaching Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act and ordered the decision published, with the company no longer named after two years.

The ICO fined LastPass UK Ltd £1,228,283 under the UK GDPR after two linked security incidents in 2022 in which a threat actor reached the company's backup database holding customer data. The ICO found that LastPass let senior staff reach corporate credentials from personal devices and encouraged linking of employee business and personal accounts. It held these practices were not appropriate technical and organisational measures under Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1). About 1.63 million UK data subjects were affected. The ICO treated the case as serious but, in setting the amount, took account of the sophisticated attack and the company's zero-knowledge encryption of vault contents.
The DPA issued a reprimand to a municipality for failing to prevent its employees from misusing their access to the National Register for private purposes.

The DPA fined a journalist €80 for unlawfully disclosing the identity of a data subject on the journalist’s social media profile after the data subject had reported them for a parking violation at a Christmas market.
The DPA closed its investigation of the Swedish Social Insurance Agency’s use of risk profiles based on machine learning since the agency already stopped the processing.

After a cyberattack gave unauthorised access to personal data of many employees, clients and collaborators (identification data, salaries, bank accounts) and restricted the controller's access to its own IT infrastructure, the Romanian authority investigated following the controller's breach notification. It found the controller had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures nor regularly tested their effectiveness. It fined the controller RON 40,663 (about EUR 8,000) and ordered it to implement appropriate measures, including multi-factor authentication for remote accounts and a password complexity policy.
The DPA fined an adult ad network for placing advertising cookies without consent, unlawfully relying on legitimate interest and lacking an EU representative.

The DPA held that a court-appointed psychologist can act as a controller and found a violation of Article 12(3) GDPR because the psychologist failed to respond to a data subject's access request without informing about the reasons for inaction.

The Garante learned through a report that the municipality of Orte had installed video surveillance cameras without ensuring transparency towards data subjects. The investigation found 43 cameras, operated without a sufficient legal basis, with deficient information notices and no data protection impact assessment, and the municipality also failed to fully and promptly answer the Authority's information requests. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 for the video surveillance conduct and EUR 1,000 for the failure to cooperate, EUR 6,000 in total. No further corrective measures were ordered because the cameras were no longer active, and the order is to be published.

The DPA issued a warning to the controller for violating Articles 5(1)(c), 15(1) and (3) and 12(2) and (6) GDPR by failing to provide access to the data subject’s personal data and by requiring unnecessary additional information for access.

The DPA ordered the operator of a live-streaming website to change their cookie banner due to its deceptive design. The DPA considered the “accept” option to be visually more prominent, unlawfully nudging users towards consent.

Romania's data protection authority, acting as lead authority, investigated Klass Wagen S.R.L. after the company notified a personal data breach and the authority received a referral. A former employee had disclosed colleagues' credentials for the contract management system, which allowed unauthorised access to the personal data of a very large number of customers and employees, including people in other EU/EEA states. The incident was reported late internally, so no immediate measures were taken. The authority found a breach of Art. 32(1)(b) and (d) and (2) GDPR, fined the company 35,615 lei (about EUR 7,000), and ordered it to put in place a procedure for revoking access rights and deactivating former employees' accounts.

The DPA imposed a €1,000 fine on a controller for unlawfully refusing to provide access to a data subject. The DPA found that the request was not abusive, unfounded or would adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others.

The DPA held that, even though a complaint against a medical doctor, who had allegedly accessed medical files without authorization, was later withdrawn, his failure to cooperate with the DPA still justified issuing a reprimand.
The DPA found a violation of a former pupil’s right to erasure because a regional education authority failed to delete their records after they completed compulsory schooling.

The DPA imposed a €150 fine on an inspector of the State Police for unlawfully obtaining a citizen’s personal data from the database of the Ministry of the Interior, and sharing it in a Discord group.

At the end of 2024 a large personal data leak affecting almost all Latvian municipalities was found; the data were stored in an information system run by ZZ Dats. The Data State Inspectorate inspected and found that the company breached Article 32 GDPR because it had not sufficiently ensured that processor obligations were met. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 300,000, calculated under the Inspectorate's methodology based on EDPB guidelines. The company has appealed to the Riga City Court. The municipalities involved received reprimands for insufficient oversight of the processor.

The DPA held that a publisher of console games could comply with an access request by providing a user with remote access via their user account. However, the DPA found that information was incomplete and found a violation of Article 15 GDPR.

The DPA fined a controller €1,500 for unlawfully recording a public sidewalk with a CCTV camera and for publishing images of a suspected thief on social media, thereby breaching the principles of data minimisation and transparency, as well as the rules governing the processing of criminal data.

The DPA held that a public service broadcaster lawfully required users to login to a streaming service in order to offer a personalised experience. According to the DPA, the processing of users’ data was necessary for the public interest and was covered by users’ expectations.

The Polish data protection authority opened proceedings of its own motion against a court bailiff after being told that personal data had been disclosed to an unauthorised recipient. The bailiff had neither reported the breach to the authority within 72 hours nor notified the person whose data was disclosed. The President of UODO found infringements of Articles 33(1) and 34(1)-(2) GDPR and imposed two separate fines, PLN 7,700 and PLN 13,200 (PLN 20,900 in total). The bailiff was also ordered to notify the affected person within 3 days with the information required by Article 34(2).

Parents complained that a secondary school published on its website a circular convening an extraordinary class council for disciplinary proceedings against their son, with the pupil's surname in the file name. The Garante found unlawful dissemination of a minor's data without a legal basis (Art. 5(1)(a), 6 GDPR, Art. 2-ter Code) and a failure to appoint a DPO and notify contact details until after the proceedings began (Art. 37(1) and (7)). The complaint-related Art. 12 charge was dropped as the school removed the file promptly in good faith. Two separate fines of EUR 2,000 each were imposed, totalling EUR 4,000, with publication of the order.

A former employee of the municipality of Curtarolo complained that CCTV footage and a video filmed by a private individual on the mayor's instruction were used against her in disciplinary proceedings, and that the municipality's CCTV system lacked proper signage and compliance. The Garante found unlawful processing on two separate conducts: street CCTV without a valid legal basis, proper information notices or a DPIA, and use of video in the employment context for disciplinary purposes without labour-law safeguards, including investigative filming outside working hours. It imposed fines of EUR 5,000 and EUR 10,000, totalling EUR 15,000, and ordered publication. No further corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ceased and the municipality said it had taken remedial steps.

A man complained that an online news article about his criminal conviction was still available long after the events, and that the publisher ignored his request of August 2024 to exercise his rights. The publisher's website had no privacy policy or contact details, and the publisher also ignored the Garante's request for information. The article was de-indexed and a privacy policy was published only after proceedings began. The Garante found violations of Article 12(1), (2) and (3) GDPR and Article 157 of the Italian Code, ordered the publisher to put in place measures to facilitate data subject requests, and fined it EUR 20,000.

A person complained that the Latina Bar Association's website published a court hearing schedule PDF containing personal data of the complainant and others, including data on criminal offences and proceedings. The PDF, listing 18 defendants and 4 defence lawyers, stayed online and was indexed by search engines for a long period. The Bar Association blamed human error during the Covid-19 emergency. The Garante found the processing unlawful, lacking a legal basis and breaching the lawfulness principle and Article 10, and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000. No further corrective measures were ordered because the online dissemination had ended.

The DPA fined the Italian public broadcast €150,000 for airing a private conversation of a former Minister involved in a political scandal. The DPA held that broadcasting the conversation was not essential to the journalistic activities of the controller.

The DPA found that the Moderate Party's national organization unlawfully processed personal data with the distribution of personal video greetings, via SMS or email, ahead of an upcoming election. Amongst other things, the political party failed to inform data subjects about the processing of their data.

The DPA found that the Sweden Democrats unlawfully sent text messages advertising for votes in an upcoming election. Amongst other things, the political party failed to inform data subjects about the processing of their data.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation in September 2025 into the electricity producer and supplier Hidroelectrica, started after the company notified a personal data breach. A technical error in the IT system used to send invoices caused a customer to receive an invoice belonging to another person, so several customers' data were disclosed without authorisation. The authority found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (d) and (4) GDPR and fined the company RON 25,392 (about EUR 5,000).
